analysis.one_liner: Bars members of Congress and their families from buying individual stocks and requires photo ID to vote in federal elections.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 232-198 on July 22, 2026, with all 218 voting Republicans in favor and 198 of 212 voting Democrats opposed; the bill now sits on the Senate calendar with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill's first section bans members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying individual stocks, and requires them to publicly disclose any planned sale 7 to 14 days in advance. Violations bring a fee that includes giving up any profits made. But the bill also contains a second, unrelated section requiring voters to show photo ID to vote in federal elections, with a narrow process for people who cannot get one. That combination is why the House vote split almost entirely by party: Republicans supported the package, and Democrats opposed it, nearly unanimously.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters worried about members of Congress profiting from their own legislative work gain new restrictions: members and their families can no longer buy individual stocks, must announce stock sales publicly before selling, and must forfeit profits from violations. The photo ID section benefits people who believe photo ID deters voting fraud.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters concerned about congressional stock trading

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children are prohibited from purchasing stocks of publicly traded companies or similar investments, including derivatives like options.
Before any covered sale, the member must file a public notice with the Clerk of the House or Secretary of the Senate 7 to 14 days ahead, which is published online.
Violations carry a fee of the greater of $2,000 or 10% of the transaction value, plus any net gain realized, and the fee cannot be paid from campaign donations or official office allowances.
The ethics office can refer a former member who resigns or retires without paying the fee to the Department of Justice.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who give up buying individual stocks and face fees for violations, and voters who lack a valid photo ID, who must cast a provisional ballot and produce ID (or sign an affidavit citing a religious objection to being photographed) within 3 days for their ballot to count.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress; voters without photo ID

drawbacks.text: The voter ID section is unrelated to stock trading: it requires a valid physical photo ID to vote in federal elections, and a provisional ballot only counts if the voter presents ID within 3 days (or attests to a religious objection to being photographed), which opponents of photo ID laws say blocks some eligible voters.

The stock restrictions stop short of a full ban: members may still sell stocks they already own (with advance notice), keep widely held funds, and spouses and dependent children can trade freely when it is part of their own job or compensation, leaving room for family trading to continue.
Enforcement is a fee collected by the ethics office, not a criminal penalty, and sales only require advance notice rather than being prohibited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stock-trading provisions address a widely criticized loophole — lawmakers trading companies they legislate on — but are weaker than a full ban, since selling remains legal with notice and spouses get broad occupational exemptions. The photo ID rider is the bigger controversy: it bundles a voting restriction into an ethics bill, which is why the bill split almost perfectly by party despite its anti-corruption purpose.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on July 22, 2026, on a nearly party-line vote, and the Senate has read it twice and placed it on its calendar, but no Senate vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: The House Committee on House Administration considered the bill at a markup on January 14, 2026, and ordered it reported as amended on a 7-4 vote; it was reported on February 3, 2026.
On July 22, 2026, the House considered the bill under a closed rule from the Rules Committee, meaning no floor amendments were allowed.
A motion by Rep. Magaziner to send the bill back to committee failed 211-218, with all 211 voting Democrats in favor and all 217 voting Republicans opposed.
The bill passed the House 232-198: 218 of 218 voting Republicans and the sole voting Independent supported it, while only 13 of 212 voting Democrats did.
The Senate received the bill on July 23, 2026, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 548) on August 6, 2026.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has fully come out ahead: supporters of congressional stock restrictions got House passage, while opponents of the voter ID rider got a bill that must still clear the Senate, where no vote has been scheduled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — Senate has not acted

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their families
industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to buy individual stocks and imposes fees on violations, but leaves selling legal with advance notice and exempts spousal trading tied to their own occupations. Because it governs officeholders themselves, the people regulated are the people voting on the bill.

The bill requires them to verify photo ID for federal elections and provide free public access to devices that scan or copy photo ID, adding administrative duties and costs. Whether this helps or burdens voters depends on how many lack ID.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Senate calendar under General Orders. Because the House passed it with only 13 Democratic votes, it would need significant Democratic support to clear a Senate procedural vote requiring 60 senators to move forward; with no vote scheduled, the usual outcome at this stage is that the bill stays on the calendar through the end of the Congress.
